tools.name: wait
tools.description:
Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.
- Use `wait` only after `exec` returns `Script running with cell ID ...`.
- `cell_id` identifies the running `exec` cell to resume.
- `yield_time_ms` controls how long to wait for more output before yielding again. Defaults to 10000 ms.
- `max_tokens` limits how much new output this wait call returns. Defaults to 10000 tokens.
- `terminate: true` stops the running cell; false or omitted waits for output.
- `wait` returns only the new output since the last yield, or the final completion or termination result for that cell.
- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
- If the cell has already finished, `wait` returns the completed result and closes the cell.

cell_id.description: Identifier of the running exec cell.

max_tokens.description: Output token budget for this wait call. Defaults to 10000 tokens.

terminate.description: True stops the running exec cell; false or omitted waits for output.

yield_time_ms.description: Wait before yielding more output. Defaults to 10000 ms.

tools.description:
Control native apps or browsers on the user’s computer by reading or operating UI. Prefer purpose-built skills, connectors, APIs, or CLIs when available.

On the first invocation of `cua_repl`, or after resetting it, execute exactly one of the API calls shown below, optionally assigning its result to a variable. Do not add other API calls, waits, or snapshots to that invocation.
The tool result will include documentation and, when creating or selecting a tab or selecting an app, its initial UI state. Selecting a browser does not open a tab. Read that result before continuing.
Use only APIs described in the tool instructions or returned documentation.

When you need an inventory of available apps, browsers, and tabs, get a snapshot of all enabled surfaces. Otherwise, use the relevant entry point below:

```javascript
await cua.getState();
```

Use the first matching browser control option from the user's request:

For a tab @-mention (`mention=tab-v1`):
Pass the complete `plugin://...` URL to get the referenced tab.

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab({ mention: tabMentionUrl });
```

For an existing tab identified by URL in browser context (including the current IAB tab):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab({ url }, { browser: browserId });
```

Known tab ID (`tabId` or `providerTabId`) and browser (name or browser @-mention):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab(tabId, { browser: browserId });
```

To open a URL in the in-app browser (`@Browser`):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.createBrowserTab("iab", url, { visible: boolean });
```

To open a URL in another named browser: pass its name directly; do not call `getBrowser` first.

```javascript
let tab = await cua.createBrowserTab(browserName, url, browserOptions);
```

Known URL, only when the user has not specified a browser by name or @-mention:

```javascript
let browser = await cua.getBrowser({ url });
```

Browser IDs and options:

- `"mcpapps"`: use `cua.getBrowser({ id: "mcpapps" })` for existing full-screen MCP Apps in the task’s side panel.
- `"iab"` (in-app browser): in `createBrowserTab`, use `visible: true` to show the browser; `false` to keep it hidden.
- `"dot"` (Dot): use only when present in browser inventory. It accesses tabs on Dot's active main thread. `cua.getTab(tabId, { browser: "dot" })` selects an existing tab. `cua.createBrowserTab("dot", url, { visible: boolean })` creates one with the same visibility options as `"iab"`.
- `"chrome"` (@Chrome), `"edge"` (@Edge): pass a short, emoji-prefixed `sessionName` (e.g. `"🔎 Task"`) to `createBrowserTab` when starting a task.

If the user specifies an app to use, get the app by name, bundle ID, or path:

```javascript
let app = await cua.getApp("Example App");
```

To add other content to the tool result, use `nodeRepl.write(value)` for text or other values and `await nodeRepl.emitImage(image)` for images. The APIs listed above already display their documentation or UI state; do not wrap their results in `write` or `emitImage`.

If your context begins with a summary of an existing computer use task, call `await cua.rewriteDocumentation()` before continuing the computer use task to ensure you have a complete view of the necessary documentation.

Several `cua_repl.js` calls may work toward the same goal. As soon as you observe the final outcome of the CUA part of the task, your next output item must be a standalone assistant commentary message containing only `::browser-complete{title="<headline>"}`. Emit it exactly once. Do this before using another tool for the next part of the user’s request or sending your reply, even if the overall request continues. If you hand control to the user, wait to summarize until the handoff has ended and you’ve observed the final outcome of the CUA part of the task. Follow the commentary in the same response with your next tool call or final answer.

Write a headline for the observed outcome in three to six words total. Start with a past-tense verb and name the result in plain language, as in 'Booked a plumber for Thursday' or 'Renewed vehicle registration'. Leave identifiers, values, and explanations for the reply. This tool is part of plugin `unified-computer-use`.

code.description: JavaScript to execute using the initialized cua_repl runtime.

timeout_ms.description: Optional execution timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000 (30 seconds) when omitted.

title.description: Short user-facing description of what this code block is doing. Prefer a few words in present-progressive form, such as 'Checking the mobile layout' or 'Comparing prices', over imperative or past-tense titles.

tools.description: Reset the persistent cua_repl JavaScript session. All JavaScript bindings are discarded. The next cua_repl.js call initializes a fresh runtime for the enabled surfaces. Brief: lattice-Boltzmann close-ups for a museum explainer. Is the setup well-posed, and what can we claim?

Context. This is a static website for the Mercedes-Benz Museum. Four exhibits get a precomputed airflow close-up, each showing two cases:
- 190 E Evo II rear-wing flap, down vs raised
- Evo II front splitter lip, in vs 40 mm forward
- Evo II front wheel arch (one state only)
- W 196 R front wheel, enclosed vs exposed

The claims are deliberately small: only the sign of a change, and only if it repeats on two grids. Computing is offline on one 10-core Mac, with our own Node.js solvers: about 16 M cell-updates/s in 2-D and about 30 M/s in 3-D. A fine-grid run takes 1–3 hours.

Numerics, common to both solvers
- BGK collision with Smagorinsky eddy viscosity (C_s = 0.16).
- Half-way bounce-back on the body. The road is a moving wall at u = U, in the car's frame.
- Free-slip top (3-D also free-slip side, and a mirror plane at the centreline).
- Inlet: equilibrium populations at ρ = 1, u = U, imposed every step, so density and velocity are both fixed.
- Outlet: zero-gradient (copies the last interior column).
- Reynolds number is held at a nominal value across grids by scaling ν with the cell size. Statistics: settle for several flow-throughs, then three averaging windows of one flow-through each.

Problem 1 (main): 2-D splitter section (D2Q9)
- Geometry: the centre-plane nose profile, traced from a photo. The body top is at 744 mm and the floor (ride height) at 120 mm; the lip is 25 mm thick. The body runs from the nose through the outlet, so it is effectively semi-infinite.
- Domain: 1.0 m ahead of the bumper face, 1.6 m behind it, 2.5 m tall. The body blocks about 30 % of the height, and the under-floor gap is a 120 mm channel driven by the moving road.
- Parameters: U = 0.1 (Ma ≈ 0.17); Re = 10⁴ on 1 m.
  - 5 mm cells: ν = 0.002, τ = 0.506.
  - 2.5 mm cells: ν = 0.004, τ = 0.512.
- Observations:
  - Pressure level: the interior sits 2–4 q∞ above the inlet density. Three cells behind the inlet there is already a vertical gradient of about 0.9 q∞. Referenced to the mean density at that inlet column (what our live tunnel uses), the lip's upper face reads cp ≈ 1.2 (not physically ≤ 1). So absolute cp is unusable.
  - Drift: the lower-face pressure keeps rising monotonically in every window. Lip in: 0.72 → 0.80 → 0.86. Lip forward: −0.16 → 0.02 → 0.18. The difference across the lip (upper minus lower, which needs no reference) is larger with the lip forward in every window, but that excess shrinks: 0.99 → 0.85 → 0.74. This was after 3 flow-throughs of settling.
  - Failed variant: ending the floor 0.5 m behind the bumper (a step up to 560 mm, open underneath) made the run diverge (NaN) within about 3 flow-throughs.
- Questions:
  a. Is the drift physical (the under-floor channel filling or emptying on a long time scale), or an artefact of the inlet fixing both ρ and u while the outlet pressure floats? Would a velocity inlet with free density (Zou–He), a pressure outlet, or a sponge zone fix the reference and the drift?
  b. What is the minimal well-posed 2-D section for a lip study?
     - Full-length car section with a closed tail and wake, versus a truncated body?
     - How far upstream should the inlet be, and how tall the domain, to keep blockage effects below the case-to-case difference?
  c. Is "upper minus lower face pressure, averaged over a fixed chord interval" a sound proxy for lip load? And is "sign agrees on both grids, and the change beats the drift between first and last window" a defensible stationarity test? If not, what is (a time scale estimate, a batch-means method)?

Problem 2: 3-D front-corner tunnels (D3Q19, half car mirrored)
- Setup:
  - U = 0.08, Re = 10⁴ on the 680 mm tyre diameter.
  - Cells of 24 mm (τ ≈ 0.5007) and 16 mm (τ ≈ 0.501), so the closure does essentially all the dissipation.
  - The tyre is still and lifted 48 mm above the road, so there is no contact-patch staircase; it is only 6–9 cells wide.
  - Domains are about 4.4 × 1.8 × 1.4 m (half width), so blockage is substantial; larger-domain runs are under way.
- Metric: width of the band where the time-mean |u| < 0.8U, on a fixed line at hub height 0.7 m behind the axle.
- Results:
  - W 196 R exposed: 574–806 mm (24 mm grid).
  - W 196 R enclosed: 830–870 mm (24 mm) and 826–858 mm (16 mm).
  - Evo arch: a path seeded in line with the tyre is shifted 377 mm outward at the station (24 mm grid); the three windows read 367–377 mm.
- Questions:
  d. At τ → 0.5 with this resolution, is a two-grid check at fixed nominal Re meaningful? The filter width scales with h, so the effective Re differs. What should be held fixed instead?
  e. Is the wake-width metric robust to blockage and to the still, lifted tyre? Would you pick a different observable for "enclosed vs exposed wheel"?

Problem 3: what to compare
6. Evo arch: the mesh's flared arch already sits at the tyre's outer face, and a narrower arch would expose the tyre, so there is no physical second case. Is there a meaningful variant at this resolution (for example, an open versus closed wheelhouse face), or is a single traced path the honest lesson?
7. Wing: the wing view is a crop of an earlier whole-car run (28 and 40 mm grids). The mean flow direction above the trailing edge goes from −8.6° to +4.0° on the 28 mm grid and from −2.3° to +5.7° on the 40 mm grid: the sign agrees, the size does not. Is a local wing solve with an inlet sampled from the whole-car field worth it, or is the sign the most this geometry (a game mesh) can support anyway?

What we need back: boundary-condition and domain changes for the 2-D section that remove the drift and fix the pressure reference; a defensible stationarity and grid criterion within a budget of a few CPU-hours per part; and a yes or no on whether each claimed sign is supportable.

L11@P0-1: 1Rigorous assessment of uncertainty is crucial to the utility of DNS results. Uncertainties in the computed statistics arise from two sources: finite statistical sampling
L12@P1: and the discretization of the Navier–Stokes equations. Due to the presence of nontrivial sampling error, standard techniques for estimating discretization error (such as
L13@P1: Richardson extrapolation) fail or are unreliable. This work provides a systematic and
L14@P1: unified approach for estimating these errors. First, a sampling error estimator that
L15@P1: accounts for correlation in the input data is developed. Then, this sampling error estimate is used as part of a Bayesian extension of Richardson extrapolation in order to
L16@P1: characterize the discretization error. These methods are tested using the Lorenz equations and are shown to perform well. These techniques are then used to investigate
L17@P1: the sampling and discretization errors in the DNS of a wall-bounded turbulent flow at
L18@P1: Reτ ≈ 180. Both small (Lx/δ ×Lz/δ = 4π ×2π) and large (Lx/δ ×Lz/δ = 12π ×4π)
L19@P1: domain sizes are investigated. For each case, a sequence of meshes was generated
L20@P1: by first designing a “nominal” mesh using standard heuristics for wall-bounded simulations. These nominal meshes were then coarsened to generate a sequence of grid
L21@P1: resolutions appropriate for the Bayesian Richardson extrapolation method. In addition, the small box case is computationally inexpensive enough to allow simulation
L22@P1: on a finer mesh, enabling the results of the extrapolation to be validated in a weak
L23@P1: sense. For both cases, it is found that while the sampling uncertainty is large enough
L24@P1: to make the order of accuracy difficult to determine, the estimated discretization
L25@P1: errors are quite small. This indicates that the commonly used heuristics provide adequate resolution for this class of problems. However, it is also found that, for some
L26@P1: quantities, the discretization error is not small relative to sampling error, indicating
L27@P1: that the conventional wisdom that sampling error dominates discretization error for
L28@P1: this class of simulations needs to be reevaluated.

L33@P1-2: 2I. INTRODUCTION
L34@P2: Direct numerical simulation (DNS) of turbulence is a valuable tool for the study of turbulent flows. Statistical quantities computed from DNS results are commonly used both
L35@P2: to further understanding of flow physics and test hypotheses regarding turbulence2,31,37 as
L36@P2: well as to calibrate and validate engineering turbulence models13,21,39,42,51. DNS data are
L37@P2: thus commonly used like experimental data. Therefore, as with experimental data, to have
L38@P2: confidence in the interpretation of a DNS or in the meaning of any comparison with DNS
L39@P2: data, one must understand the uncertainty in that data. However, it is not common in the
L40@P2: DNS literature to report these uncertainties because uncertainties in the data are generally
L41@P2: not systematically evaluated. Instead, it is common for expert practitioners to determine
L42@P2: grid spacing requirements, required simulation time, etc. based on a combination of knowledge gained from previous experience and observations of simulation outputs. The goal of
L43@P2: this work is to improve upon this practice by providing a systematic method for estimating
L44@P2: uncertainty in the statistics computed from DNS data.
L45@P2: Uncertainty estimation for DNS is an example of solution verification for the DNS statistical quantities. The goal of solution verification is to ensure that numerical solutions of
L46@P2: a mathematical model are sufficiently accurate approximations to the exact solution of the
L47@P2: model1,40. Solution verification techniques for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) have
L48@P2: been the topic of a large body of research38,45,47. The simplest techniques in this domain
L49@P2: are based on Richardson extrapolation for estimating discretization error given a sequence
L50@P2: of simulations on successively finer meshes. However, these developments have had little
L51@P2: impact on the practice of DNS due to the fact that the outputs are generally statistical
L52@P2: quantities that are contaminated not only by discretization error but also by sampling error.
L53@P2: Since the goal of DNS is to resolve all relevant physical scales, it is generally expected that
L54@P2: errors due to finite sampling are significant relative to discretization errors. Thus, simple
L55@P2: methods for estimating discretization error that are common for other CFD calculations, like
L56@P2: Richardson extrapolation, are not directly applicable to DNS results, because the estimated
L57@P2: discretization error is greatly affected by sampling error. The result is that, while systematic mesh resolution studies have been performed19, it is not common to actually estimate
L58@P2: discretization error.
L59@P2: To address this issue, it is of primary importance to estimate sampling errors. Of course,
L60@P2-3: 3if the data used to compute the statistics were samples from independent, identically distributed random variables, the central limit theorem allows easy estimation of the sampling
L61@P3: error. However, the samples used to generate DNS statistics are drawn from a time history
L62@P3: and/or spatial field and are generally not independent. To reduce the correlation, the samples used to compute statistics are sometimes taken “far” apart in time and then treated
L63@P3: as independent19. While this procedure has intuitive appeal, it can lead to underestimated
L64@P3: uncertainty if the snapshots are not sufficiently separated. Alternatively, if the snapshots
L65@P3: are taken too far apart, it leads to fewer samples and overestimates of sampling error.
L66@P3: Instead of restricting the samples in this way, it is preferable to use all the available
L67@P3: data and account for correlations. One approach to accounting for the correlations in DNS
L68@P3: statistics, which was proposed by Hoyas and Jiménez27, uses a sequence of “coarse grainings”
L69@P3: of the data. However, our experience has been that it is difficult to automate this procedure
L70@P3: because the presence of noise often requires both user intervention and interpretation.
L71@P3: A more promising approach based on direct estimation of the correlations in the data
L72@P3: has been used to estimate sampling errors in many fields, including the weather and climate
L73@P3: communities50,53. In this approach, the autocorrelation of the data, which is not known
L74@P3: a priori, must be estimated from the data, which presents its own challenges. Here, we
L75@P3: follow the work of Broersen9,10 and fit autoregressive models from which the autocorrelation
L76@P3: function is then computed.
L77@P3: Given an estimate of the sampling error, discretization errors are estimated using data
L78@P3: from simulations with different resolution levels. As noted earlier, because sampling uncertainty is generally expected to be of the same magnitude as the discretization error, at least
L79@P3: for grid spacing and time steps used for production DNS, standard Richardson extrapolation
L80@P3: generally fails to correctly estimate the discretization error. Here, a Bayesian extension of
L81@P3: the standard Richardson extrapolation that accounts for both statistical uncertainty and
L82@P3: prior information (e.g., the expected asymptotic order of accuracy) is formulated. This
L83@P3: Bayesian statistical formulation effectively regularizes the Richardson extrapolation problem to decrease the sensitivity of the estimated discretization error to finite sampling effects.
L84@P3: The performance of these estimators is tested using the Lorenz equations. They are then
L85@P3: applied to the problem of assessing uncertainties in statistics from the DNS of incompressible, turbulent channel flow at Reτ ≈ 180. The resulting discretization error estimates are
L86@P3: assessed using a small domain case where it is feasible to run a simulation with twice the
L87@P3-4: 4resolution of the nominal simulation, which is designed according to typical DNS heuristics.
L88@P4: For many quantities, including the mean velocity, Reynolds shear stress, and skin friction
L89@P4: coefficient, the discretization error model is validated, meaning that its predictions agree with
L90@P4: the observations at higher resolution. For these quantities, the model is then used to predict
L91@P4: the discretization error present in a large domain simulation with resolution again set by
L92@P4: the usual heuristics. The results demonstrate that, for these quantities, the discretization
L93@P4: errors are small, generally much less than one percent. Thus, the usual mesh heuristics
L94@P4: appear to be adequate. It should be pointed out however that the estimated discretization
L95@P4: error is often similar to or larger than the estimated sampling error. This result violates
L96@P4: the conventional wisdom that sampling error dominates, indicating that it is important to
L97@P4: systematically estimate discretization error effects as well.
L98@P4: Unfortunately, for other quantities, including the streamwise velocity variance and the
L99@P4: vorticity variances, our simple discretization error model is invalidated by the high resolution
L100@P4: small domain simulation results. While the observed changes between the nominal and high
L101@P4: resolution simulation are small, and so there is no indication that the nominal resolution
L102@P4: is inadequate, this invalidation precludes the use of the model to predict the discretization
L103@P4: error with any confidence. Thus, no discretization error estimates are presented for these
L104@P4: quantities.
L105@P4: The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. The full error estimation methodology
L106@P4: is presented in §II, including the sampling error estimation (§II A), the Bayesian Richardson
L107@P4: extrapolation procedure (§II B), and the illustrative Lorenz example (§II C). Results for DNS
L108@P4: of Reτ = 180 channel flow are given in §III, and §IV provides conclusions.
L109@P4: II. METHODOLOGY
L110@P4: This work addresses two major sources of uncertainty in statistics computed from DNS:
L111@P4: finite sampling error and discretization error. The sampling error estimator is described
L112@P4: briefly in §II A. This estimate is then used in a Bayesian extension of Richardson extrapolation to determine probabilistic estimates of the discretization error and the exact value of the
L113@P4: statistic of interest, as described in §II B. To assess the characteristics of these procedures
L114@P4: in a simple setting where different regimes can easily be explored, both estimators are used
L115@P4: to evaluate simulations of the Lorenz equations in §II C.
